chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Building Blocks of a DCF

lessons.title: Free Cash Flow to the Firm vs Free Cash Flow to Equity

children.text: A business generates cash, but that cash does not all belong to shareholders. Lenders have a claim first, in the form of interest and repayments. Before you build a DCF, you must decide whose cash you are valuing. Get this choice wrong and the model can look perfectly reasonable while producing a number that means nothing.

body.text: Match the cash flow to the people who own it. Cash flow to the firm belongs to lenders and shareholders together, is discounted at WACC and gives enterprise value. Cash flow to equity belongs to shareholders alone, is discounted at the cost of equity and gives equity value.

children.text: Two Claims on the Same Cash

Picture a cement company that has funded its plants partly with ₹1,500 crore of bank loans and NCDs, and partly with shareholders' money. Every rupee of cash the plants generate eventually flows to one of these two groups.
Free cash flow to the firm (FCFF)
is the cash available to everyone who funded the business, before a single rupee goes to lenders.

markDefs.definition: Cash generated by the business after taxes, capital expenditure and working capital needs, but before any payments to lenders. It is available to all providers of capital, debt and equity together.

children.text: Free cash flow to equity (FCFE)
is what is left for shareholders after lenders have been paid interest and any net debt repayments, and after any new borrowing has come in.

markDefs.definition: Cash left for shareholders after the business has paid taxes, capital expenditure, working capital needs, interest and debt repayments, and received any new borrowing.

children.text: Discount FCFF and you get the value of the whole business, its
enterprise value
. Discount FCFE and you get only the shareholders' slice, equity value. Both routes should land on the same equity value per share if the assumptions are consistent.

markDefs.definition: The value of a company's operating business to all capital providers. Enterprise value minus net debt (debt less cash) equals equity value.

children.text: Calculating FCFF

body.caption: Operating profit after tax, plus non-cash charges, minus reinvestment

cells: Operating profit after tax, as if the company had no debt. Also called NOPAT.
Profit and loss statement: profit before interest and tax, then apply the tax rate
Depreciation and amortisation, added back because no cash left the business
Profit and loss statement or cash flow statement
Cash spent on plants, machinery, stores, software and other long-term assets
Investing activities: purchase of property, plant and equipment and intangibles
Increase in net working capital: more receivables and inventory, less supplier credit
Working capital changes in operating activities, or the balance sheet

body.text: Why tax EBIT and not PAT? Because FCFF is meant to be the cash the business would generate if it had no debt. The tax benefit of interest is not ignored. It is captured later, in the after-tax cost of debt inside WACC. Counting it in both places is a classic double count.

children.text: Calculating FCFE

body.caption: Net borrowing = new debt raised minus debt repaid

children.text: Equivalently, starting from net profit: FCFE = PAT + D&A - Capex - ΔNWC + Net borrowing. Both formulas give the same answer, because PAT is already after interest and tax.
Worked Example: Kaveri Ridge Cement

Kaveri Ridge Cement Ltd is a fictional NSE-listed cement maker in Karnataka. It is expanding clinker capacity, partly funded with a new term loan. For simplicity, we use a 25% tax rate. In practice, Indian companies that opt for the concessional corporate tax regime pay an effective rate of about 25.17% including surcharge and cess.

body.caption: Kaveri Ridge Cement: FCFF and FCFE for the year (₹ crore, illustrative)

cells: Less increase in net working capital

children.text: Check it from the net profit route: PAT ₹660 + D&A ₹300 - capex ₹450 - ΔNWC ₹50 + net borrowing ₹100 = ₹560 crore. Same answer.

body.text: Notice that FCFE (₹560 crore) is higher than FCFF (₹550 crore) this year. That is only because Kaveri Ridge borrowed ₹100 crore more than it repaid. Borrowing can make FCFE look healthy in any single year. Never project a year of heavy borrowing forward as if it were sustainable cash for shareholders.

children.text: Starting From an Indian Cash Flow Statement

You will rarely have a clean EBIT-to-FCFF build handed to you. More often you start from cash flow from operations (CFO) on screener.in or in the annual report. One Indian presentation detail changes the formula.
Under
Ind AS 7

, most Indian non-financial companies report interest paid under financing activities, not operating activities. Their CFO is therefore before interest, but after actual taxes paid, which were reduced by the interest deduction.

markDefs.definition: The Indian Accounting Standard on cash flow statements. It allows interest paid to be classified under operating or financing activities, and most Indian non-financial companies show it under financing.

body.caption: Formulas from CFO, depending on where interest paid sits

cells: CFO - Capex - Interest paid + Net borrowing

body.title: Show me Kaveri Ridge from its cash flow statement

children.text: Kaveri Ridge shows interest paid under financing activities. Its CFO = EBIT ₹1,000 - taxes paid ₹220 + D&A ₹300 - ΔNWC ₹50 = ₹1,030 crore.

Both match the EBIT-based build. The small "Interest paid × t" deduction in FCFF removes the tax saving from interest that is already inside the taxes paid figure, so that it is not counted again in WACC.

body.text: Leases distort CFO. Since Ind AS 116 took effect for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2019, payments on most leases are shown under financing activities. For retailers, airlines, hospital chains and restaurant companies with large leased portfolios, reported CFO looks higher than the cash the business really generates. Deduct lease payments when calculating free cash flow for such companies, or treat lease liabilities as debt consistently throughout your valuation.

children.text: Discount Each Cash Flow at the Right Rate
FCFF is discounted at the
weighted average cost of capital (WACC)

, because it belongs to lenders and shareholders together. FCFE is discounted at the cost of equity, because it belongs to shareholders alone. Chapter 2 builds both rates. Here is how the two routes meet.

markDefs.definition: The blended required return of all capital providers, weighting the cost of equity and the after-tax cost of debt by their shares of total capital. Built step by step later in this chapter.

columns.label: FCFF route
points: Then: subtract net debt to get equity value
Best for: most non-financial companies, especially when debt levels will change

columns.label: FCFE route
points: Best for: companies with stable debt levels, and as a basis for valuing lenders

children.text: Both routes, one answer

Suppose Kaveri Ridge is now a mature business whose FCFF of ₹550 crore grows at 5% a year forever, and its ₹1,500 crore of net debt grows at the same 5% to keep leverage stable. That means steady-state net borrowing of ₹75 crore a year, not this year's ₹100 crore, and FCFE of ₹535 crore. Shareholders require 12%. Lenders charge 8% before tax, or 6% after tax.

body.title: Show me where the WACC of 11.02% comes from

children.text: Equity is worth ₹7642.86 crore and net debt ₹1,500 crore, so total capital is ₹9142.86 crore.

content.caption: Weights are market values of equity and debt

children.text: Enterprise value = ₹550 ÷ (11.0156% - 5%) = ₹9142.86 crore. Subtract net debt of ₹1,500 crore and equity value is ₹7642.86 crore, identical to the FCFE route. The routes agree because the discount rates and the borrowing assumption are consistent with each other.
The Five Most Common Mismatches

body.caption: Errors that make a DCF meaningless

cells: WACC is lower than the cost of equity, so equity value is overstated. In the example above, by 16%.
Discounting FCFF at the cost of equity
Uses too high a rate on cash that partly belongs to lenders, and the result is neither enterprise nor equity value
Enterprise value is presented as if it all belonged to shareholders. The more indebted the company, the bigger the error.
FCFE inflated by one year of heavy borrowing is treated as recurring cash for shareholders
Lease payments sit in financing activities, so free cash flow is overstated for lease-heavy businesses

children.text: Check Your Understanding

body.title: Calculate FCFF
body.prompt: A pharma company reports EBIT of ₹400 crore, a tax rate of 25%, depreciation of ₹80 crore, capex of ₹120 crore and an increase in net working capital of ₹20 crore. What is its FCFF, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: NOPAT = ₹400 × (1 - 0.25) = ₹300. FCFF = ₹300 + ₹80 - ₹120 - ₹20 = ₹240 crore. Interest is ignored at this stage because FCFF is calculated before any payments to lenders.

body.title: Pick the discount rate
body.question: You have projected a company's free cash flow to equity for the next ten years. Which rate should you discount it at, and what do you get?
options: Cost of equity, giving equity value
After-tax cost of debt, giving enterprise value
body.explanation: FCFE belongs only to shareholders, so it is discounted at the return shareholders require, the cost of equity. The result is equity value directly, with no need to subtract debt.

body.title: The FCFF route
body.textWithBlank: Discounting FCFF at WACC gives ___ value, from which you subtract net debt to reach equity value.
body.explanation: FCFF is available to all capital providers, so its present value is the value of the whole firm, enterprise value. Subtracting net debt leaves the shareholders' portion.

body.title: Reading a real-looking cash flow statement
body.scenario: Pooja, an investor in Ahmedabad, is looking at a textile exporter's latest cash flow statement on screener.in. Cash from operating activities is ₹820 crore. Under investing activities, purchase of fixed assets is ₹300 crore. Under financing activities, interest paid is ₹100 crore and the company repaid ₹150 crore more debt than it raised. The tax rate is 25%. A friend tells her, "Free cash flow is just ₹820 minus ₹300, so shareholders got ₹520 crore."
body.prompt: Calculate FCFF and FCFE correctly, and explain what her friend got wrong.
body.modelAnswer:
Interest paid sits under financing activities, so CFO is before interest but after taxes that were reduced by the interest deduction.

FCFF = CFO - Capex - Interest paid × t = ₹820 - ₹300 - (₹100 × 0.25) = ₹495 crore.

FCFE = CFO - Capex - Interest paid + Net borrowing = ₹820 - ₹300 - ₹100 - ₹150 = ₹270 crore.

Check: FCFF - Interest × (1 - t) + Net borrowing = ₹495 - ₹75 - ₹150 = ₹270 crore.

What the friend got wrong: ₹520 crore is neither measure. It ignores that interest of ₹100 crore was paid to lenders, not shareholders, and that ₹150 crore of cash went to net debt repayment. Only ₹270 crore was actually free for shareholders this year. It is also worth noting that the repayment reduced debt, so next year's interest bill and future FCFE should improve.

cards.definition: EBIT × (1 - t) + D&A - Capex - ΔNWC. Cash available to lenders and shareholders together.
FCFF - Interest × (1 - t) + Net borrowing. Cash available to shareholders only.
Net operating profit after tax: EBIT × (1 - t). Profit as if the company had no debt.
Present value of FCFF at WACC. The value of the business to all capital providers.
Enterprise value minus net debt, or the present value of FCFE at the cost of equity.
New debt raised minus debt repaid during the period. Positive net borrowing increases FCFE.
Most Indian non-financial companies show interest paid under financing activities, so their CFO is before interest.

points: FCFF is cash for lenders and shareholders together. FCFE is cash for shareholders alone.
FCFF = EBIT × (1 - t) + D&A - Capex - ΔNWC. FCFE = FCFF - Interest × (1 - t) + Net borrowing.
Discount FCFF at WACC to get enterprise value, then subtract net debt. Discount FCFE at the cost of equity to get equity value directly.
With consistent assumptions, both routes give the same equity value. Mixing cash flows and discount rates does not.
Most Indian companies show interest paid under financing activities, which changes how you calculate free cash flow from CFO.
Borrowing can inflate FCFE in any one year, and Ind AS 116 lease accounting can inflate CFO. Adjust for both.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Kaveri Ridge Cement Ltd and the individuals named are fictional, and their figures are illustrative. A simplified 25% tax rate is used throughout. Accounting and tax treatments vary by company; check the notes to the financial statements. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.
